summary.title: How to write good prompts: using spaced repetition to create understanding
summary.one_liner: Learn why spaced repetition prompts work through retrieval practice, and how to write focused, precise, tractable, effortful prompts that build real understanding, illustrated with a chicken stock recipe.
keywords: learning from articles with spaced repetition
takeaways: Each spaced repetition prompt is a recurring task, so prompt design is task design.
Effective retrieval practice prompts are focused, precise, consistent, tractable, and effortful.
Break knowledge into small discrete components and write tightly scoped questions for each.
Write prompts iteratively: aim for a small number (5-10) per pass rather than exhaustively covering a text.
Good prompts can go beyond the source text by connecting ideas to your own life and work.
summary.summary: The guide, by Andy Matuschak, explains that spaced repetition systems are only as good as their prompts and that the main mechanism behind them is retrieval practice. It lays out properties of effective prompts: focused, precise, consistent, tractable, and effortful. It then works through a concrete example, a chicken stock recipe, to show how to decompose knowledge into prompts covering facts, procedures, concepts, and personal applications. The guide ends with advice on iterative prompt-writing for articles and books, and describes the "mnemonic medium" concept behind the Orbit system.
